\begin{center}\textsc{Abstract}\end{center}
\begin{quote}
We report seven new best-known Max-$k$-Cut values on the G-set benchmark,
relative to the published results identified as of October 15, 2026.
For G81 with $k=3$, we obtain 16{,}510, exceeding 16{,}392 by 118.
For G22 with $k=4$ and G55 with $k=3$, we obtain 18{,}787 and 12{,}437,
improving the published values by 11 and 5, respectively.
For $k=5$ on G1--G4, we obtain 17{,}706, 17{,}710, 17{,}705 and 17{,}710,
improving the published values by 1, 3, 2 and 1.
The accompanying release contains 35 explicit vertex partitions: these seven
improvements, 17 matches to published best-known values (including three
provably optimal solutions), ten reference values for $k=6,8$, and one
additional G81 partition for $k=4$. The latter has value 16{,}666, below the
published Gurobi value of 16{,}670, and is not claimed as a new best-known result.
This note publishes solution certificates and their verification, while leaving
the solution-generation algorithms to a separate study.
\end{quote}
\textbf{Keywords} Max-$k$-Cut $\cdot$ G-set $\cdot$ graph partitioning $\cdot$ solution certificates.

\section{Introduction}
The G-set graphs are a widely used benchmark for Max-Cut and its generalisation,
Max-$k$-Cut~\cite{gset,moh}. Given a weighted undirected graph $G=(V,E,w)$ and
$k\ge2$, the objective is to assign each vertex to a part so as to maximise
\begin{equation}
 C(x)=\sum_{(i,j)\in E}w_{ij}[x_i\ne x_j],\qquad x\in\{0,\ldots,k-1\}^{|V|}.
 \label{eq:cut}
\end{equation}
All certificates in this release use all $k$ labels. A feasible partition gives
a lower bound on the optimum and can be checked directly from the edge list,
independently of how it was found.

This note documents seven improved values and their partitions. Its contribution
is the set of verifiable solutions and the comparison with published values;
it makes no comparative runtime or algorithmic performance claim.

\section{Published comparison values}
The multiple search operator heuristic (MOH) of Ma and Hao~\cite{moh} reports
G-set values for $k=2,3,4,5$. The $k=5$ comparisons here use the accepted
journal manuscript rather than the duplicated $k=4$ table in arXiv version~1.
Garvardt et al.~\cite{garvardt} evaluated parameterized local search (LS) and
integer linear programming (ILP) on MOH starting partitions. Their 2026 journal
version reports 16{,}392 for G81 with $k=3$ (LS, Table~7), 16{,}525 for G81
with $k=4$ (LS, Table~8), and 12{,}432 for G55 with $k=3$ (ILP, Table~7).

The parallel evolutionary algorithm framework (PEAF) of Shao and
Yang~\cite{peaf}, published online in September 2026, reports the values used
here for G1--G4 with $k=5$ (Table~21), as well as several of the matched
values (Tables~19--20). The population annealing study of Khan et al.~\cite{pamc}
also reports 12{,}432 for G55 and 17{,}169 for G22 with $k=3$ (Table~S2).

It is necessary to compare against all reported solver columns. In particular,
Shao and Wu~\cite{ode} report a Gurobi value of \textbf{16{,}670} for G81 with
$k=4$ in Table~3, higher than the LS value of 16{,}525. This published value
is included in our comparisons. No explicit partition for that external value
was independently checked in this study.

\section{Results}
\subsection{Seven improved best-known values}
Table~\ref{tab:new} lists the improvements over the highest published values
identified in the literature reviewed for this note. None of these seven
solutions is claimed to be globally optimal.
\begin{table}[ht]
\centering\small
\caption{Improved Max-$k$-Cut values. $\Delta$ is the gain over the published comparison value.}
\label{tab:new}
\begin{tabular}{lrrrrrl}
\toprule
Graph & $k$ & This work & Previous & $\Delta$ & Gain (\%) & Source\\
\midrule
G81 & 3 & \textbf{16{,}510} & 16{,}392 & +118 & 0.720 & LS~\cite{garvardt}\\
G22 & 4 & \textbf{18{,}787} & 18{,}776 & +11 & 0.059 & MOH, PEAF~\cite{moh,peaf}\\
G55 & 3 & \textbf{12{,}437} & 12{,}432 & +5 & 0.040 & ILP, PAMC~\cite{garvardt,pamc}\\
G1 & 5 & \textbf{17{,}706} & 17{,}705 & +1 & 0.006 & PEAF~\cite{peaf}\\
G2 & 5 & \textbf{17{,}710} & 17{,}707 & +3 & 0.017 & PEAF~\cite{peaf}\\
G3 & 5 & \textbf{17{,}705} & 17{,}703 & +2 & 0.011 & PEAF~\cite{peaf}\\
G4 & 5 & \textbf{17{,}710} & 17{,}709 & +1 & 0.006 & MOH, PEAF~\cite{moh,peaf}\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

G81 has 20{,}000 vertices and 40{,}000 edges, including 19{,}983 edges of
weight $-1$. Its objective is the signed sum in Eq.~\eqref{eq:cut}, not the
number of crossing edges. G22 has 2{,}000 vertices and 19{,}990 edges; G55
has 5{,}000 vertices and 12{,}498 edges; G1--G4 each have 800 vertices and
19{,}176 edges. The latter six graphs have only unit positive weights.

\subsection{Seventeen matches and three optimality certificates}
Table~\ref{tab:match} gives 17 matches to published values. The three optimal
cases are included in this count. In each of these cases all edge weights are
$+1$ and every edge crosses the partition, attaining the upper bound $|E|$.
\begin{table}[ht]
\centering\small
\caption{Partitions matching published best-known values. Values on G1--G5 are in graph order.}
\label{tab:match}
\begin{tabular}{lcll}
\toprule
Graph & $k$ & Cut values & Comparison\\
\midrule
G1--G5 & 3 & 15{,}165, 15{,}172, 15{,}173, 15{,}184, 15{,}193 & MOH, PEAF~\cite{moh,peaf}\\
G1--G5 & 4 & 16{,}804, 16{,}810, 16{,}806, 16{,}814, 16{,}816 & PEAF~\cite{peaf}\\
G5 & 5 & 17{,}711 & PEAF~\cite{peaf}\\
G22 & 3 & 17{,}169 & PEAF, PAMC~\cite{peaf,pamc}\\
G43 & 3, 4 & 8{,}573, 9{,}377 & MOH; LS/ILP, PEAF~\cite{moh,garvardt,peaf}\\
G55 & 4 & 12{,}498 & All edges cut; optimal\\
G70 & 3, 4 & 9{,}999, 9{,}999 & All edges cut; optimal\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

We did not identify directly comparable published values for G1--G5 with
$k=6$ or $k=8$ in the literature reviewed. Table~\ref{tab:reference} therefore
provides reference points, without making a claim of priority.

\caption{Reference values on G1--G5 without an identified published comparison.}
\label{tab:reference}
\begin{tabular}{rrrrrr}

$k$ & G1 & G2 & G3 & G4 & G5\\
\midrule

\subsection{Additional G81 certificate}
The release also contains our G81 partition for $k=4$, with value 16{,}666.
It is four below the published Gurobi value of 16{,}670~\cite{ode} and is
listed separately from both improvements and matches. Including this partition
brings the total number of certificates to 35.

\section{Certificate encoding and verification}
Every partition is provided as a UTF-8 text file with one integer per line:
line $i$ is the label of vertex $i$, in the original G-set numbering.
The file \texttt{results.csv} records graph size, $k$, cut value, comparison
source, and the SHA-256 digest of each certificate. Original graph files are
obtained from the Stanford G-set directory~\cite{gset}; their expected hashes
are included in the release.

The dependency-free Python verifier checks graph and solution hashes, the
number and range of labels, and Eq.~\eqref{eq:cut}. An independently written
checker additionally confirms that no single-vertex move improves any of the
35 partitions. This local optimality does not establish global optimality.
The three all-edges-cut cases have the separate upper-bound proof given above.
The checks verify the solutions, not the completeness of a literature search.

Appendix~\ref{app:certificates} embeds the seven improved partitions so that
these certificates remain available with the paper. For $k\le4$, expand each
hexadecimal digit to four bits, most significant bit first, and read each
successive pair of bits as one vertex label. For $k=5$, each hexadecimal digit
is the label of one vertex. Concatenate wrapped lines before decoding.

\section{Conclusion}
The seven improved values comprise G81 with $k=3$, G22 with $k=4$, G55 with
$k=3$, and G1--G4 with $k=5$. The explicit partitions establish their values
without access to the solution-generation algorithms. The accompanying data
also provide 17 matches, ten reference values and one additional G81
certificate, with the comparison categories kept distinct.
